title: Real Numbers: HCF, LCM and Irrational Numbers
seo_title: Real Numbers Class 10 Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 1)
standard_text: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (statements after reviewing work done earlier and after illustrating and motivating through examples); proofs of irrationality of √2, √3 and √5 (summary of the CBSE syllabus)
meta_desc: Class 10 Real Numbers worksheet (NCERT Chapter 1): prime factorisation, HCF and LCM, HCF × LCM, irrational numbers and word problems. 100 practice questions with answers, free and printable.
key_big: Every composite number = a unique product of primes
key_sub: HCF uses the smallest powers, LCM the greatest powers.
body_html:
How it works

Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way (apart from the order).

HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime.

For two numbers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.

A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q. √2, √3, √5 are irrational. Rational + irrational is irrational.

Example

Find the HCF and LCM of 96 and 404.

96 = 25 × 3, 404 = 22 × 101

HCF = 22 = 4

LCM = 25 × 3 × 101

Answer: HCF = 4, LCM = 9,696

Example

Show that 5 − √3 is irrational.

Suppose 5 − √3 = r (rational)

Then √3 = 5 − r, which is rational

Contradiction

Answer: 5 − √3 is irrational

Common mistakes

  • Taking the greatest powers for the HCF (that gives the LCM).
  • Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers. It works only for two.
  • Calling √4 or √9 irrational. They equal 2 and 3.

faq.q: What is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic?
faq.a: Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.

faq.q: How do I find the HCF and LCM by prime factorisation?
faq.a: Write each number as a product of primes. HCF: multiply the smallest power of each common prime. LCM: multiply the greatest power of every prime that appears.

faq.q: Why can 6ⁿ never end with the digit 0?
faq.a: A number ending in 0 must have both 2 and 5 as prime factors. 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no factor 5.

faq.q: How do I prove that √2 is irrational?
faq.a: Assume √2 = a/b with a and b coprime. Squaring gives a² = 2b², so 2 divides a and then 2 divides b. This contradicts that a and b are coprime.

sets.title: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation

items.q: Find the HCF of 21 and 182 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 21 = 3 × 7; 182 = 2 × 7 × 13. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 7 = 7.

items.q: Find the HCF of 60 and 84 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 60 = 22 × 3 × 5; 84 = 22 × 3 × 7. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 22 × 3 = 12.

items.q: Find the HCF of 30 and 54 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 30 = 2 × 3 × 5; 54 = 2 × 33. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 2 × 3 = 6.

items.q: Find the LCM of 15 and 72 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 15 = 3 × 5; 72 = 23 × 32. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 23 × 32 × 5 = 360.

items.q: Find the HCF of 48 and 312 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 48 = 24 × 3; 312 = 23 × 3 × 13. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 23 × 3 = 24.

items.q: Find the LCM of 84, 108 and 162 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 84 = 22 × 3 × 7; 108 = 22 × 33; 162 = 2 × 34. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 22 × 34 × 7 = 2,268.

items.q: Find the HCF of 135 and 252 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 135 = 33 × 5; 252 = 22 × 32 × 7. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 32 = 9.

items.q: Find the HCF of 39 and 72 by prime factorisation.

items.q: Find the LCM of 162 and 180 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 162 = 2 × 34; 180 = 22 × 32 × 5. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 22 × 34 × 5 = 1,620.

items.q: Find the LCM of 48, 60 and 156 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 48 = 24 × 3; 60 = 22 × 3 × 5; 156 = 22 × 3 × 13. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 24 × 3 × 5 × 13 = 3,120.

items.q: Find the LCM of 90, 125 and 135 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 90 = 2 × 32 × 5; 125 = 53; 135 = 33 × 5. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 2 × 33 × 53 = 6,750.

items.q: Find the HCF of 72, 132 and 360 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 72 = 23 × 32; 132 = 22 × 3 × 11; 360 = 23 × 32 × 5. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 22 × 3 = 12.

items.q: Find the LCM of 50 and 130 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 50 = 2 × 52; 130 = 2 × 5 × 13. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 2 × 52 × 13 = 650.

items.q: Find the HCF of 44 and 84 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 44 = 22 × 11; 84 = 22 × 3 × 7. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 22 = 4.

items.q: Find the HCF of 120 and 180 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 120 = 23 × 3 × 5; 180 = 22 × 32 × 5. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 22 × 3 × 5 = 60.

items.q: Find the LCM of 70 and 112 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 70 = 2 × 5 × 7; 112 = 24 × 7. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 24 × 5 × 7 = 560.

items.q: Find the LCM of 27, 63 and 216 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 27 = 33; 63 = 32 × 7; 216 = 23 × 33. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime = 23 × 33 × 7 = 1,512.

items.q: Find the HCF of 44 and 56 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 44 = 22 × 11; 56 = 23 × 7. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 22 = 4.

items.q: Find the HCF of 16 and 42 by prime factorisation.
items.e: 16 = 24; 42 = 2 × 3 × 7. HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime = 2 = 2.

sets.title: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers

items.q: For any two positive integers a and b, which statement is always true?
c: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a + b
HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
HCF(a, b) + LCM(a, b) = a + b
items.e: HCF × LCM = a × b. LCM = a × b only when HCF = 1. (This product rule does not hold for three numbers.)

items.q: The HCF of 44 and 12 is 4. Find their LCM.
items.e: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: LCM = 44 × 12 ÷ 4 = 132.

items.q: The HCF of 221 and 182 is 13. Find their LCM.
items.e: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: LCM = 221 × 182 ÷ 13 = 3,094.

items.q: The HCF of 81 and 99 is 9. Find their LCM.

items.q: Can two numbers have 2 as their HCF and 133 as their LCM?
c: No, because 133 is not divisible by 2
No, because the LCM must be less than 100
items.e: The HCF always divides the LCM. 133 ÷ 2 is not a whole number, so no.

items.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
items.e: √64 and √9 = 8 and 3 are rational. √2 cannot be written as p/q, so √2 is irrational.

items.q: Is (√3)² rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: (√3)² = 3, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.

items.q: Is √2 × √2 rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: √2 × √2 = 2, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.
If 4 − 2√2 = r were rational, then √2 = (rational) would be rational — a contradiction. So it is irrational.

items.q: Is √7 × √7 rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: √7 × √7 = 7, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.

items.q: Is √5 × √5 rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: √5 × √5 = 5, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.

items.q: In the proof that √3 is irrational, we assume √3 = a/b (a, b coprime). What do we show next?
c: 3 divides both a and b, which contradicts that they are coprime
a = 3 b, so √3 is an integer
a and b are both even, so √3 is even
items.e: Squaring gives a² = 3b², so 3 divides a; writing a = 3c gives b² = 3c², so 3 divides b. 3 divides both a and b — a contradiction.
If 9 + 4√7 = r were rational, then √7 = (rational) would be rational — a contradiction. So it is irrational.

items.q: Is (6 + √3)(6 − √3) rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: (6 + √3)(6 − √3) = 33, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.

items.q: Is (3 + √5)(3 − √5) rational or irrational?
items.e: Work it out: (3 + √5)(3 − √5) = 4, which is rational. A product of irrational numbers can be rational.

items.q: Three ropes are 72 m, 32 m and 76 m long. What is the greatest length (in m) of pieces that can measure all three exactly?
Three bells ring every 9, 12 and 15 minutes. They ring together at 9 a.m. After how many minutes will they next ring together?
items.e: They ring together after a common multiple of the times; the first one is the LCM(9, 12, 15) = 180 minutes.

items.q: A sweet seller has 180 kaju barfis and 414 badam barfis. He stacks them so that each stack has the same number of one kind only. What is the most barfis in each stack (fewest trays)?
items.e: HCF(180, 414) = 18 barfis per stack.
